new_statements.quote: Stress is a syllable-level phenomenon in Komnzo. A stressed syllable is marked by higher intensity and sometimes higher pitch. Vowel duration is not an acoustic correlate of stress. [...] The prosodic domain of stress asignment is the phonological word. Primary stress (marked by preceding ˈ in the examples) is assigned to the initial syllable of a word. There are a number of exceptions to initial stress which I will describe below. Secondary stress (marked by preceding ˌ in the examples) carries little function in Komnzo and it is often hard to distinguish from unstressed syllables. Secondary stress only occurs in words with more than three syllables. [...] Stress is assigned from left to right. Words with two, three, and four syllables construct a trochee, dactyl, and ditrochee, respectively. (pp. 71-72)
new_statements.citation: Döhler, Christian (2018). A grammar of Komnzo. Berlin: Language Science Press. xii+456 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable) (initial primary stress; secondary on the third syllable of four-syllable words), which is exactly Döhler's Table 2.9 trochee/dactyl/ditrochee pattern. Adds: the domain is the phonological word (proclitics excluded), duration is not a stress cue, epenthetic schwa may bear stress, final syllables never stressed, and exceptions in partial reduplication and proclitic-initial verbs; secondary stress in 5+ syllable words is variable and left open.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the phonological word, assigned left to right; 2-, 3- and 4-syllable words form a trochee, dactyl and ditrochee (ˈσσ, ˈσσσ, ˈσσˌσσ), so secondary stress lands on the third syllable of four-syllable words. Stress is cued by intensity and sometimes pitch, not duration; the epenthetic schwa can carry stress; word-final syllables are always unstressed. In verbs stress is strictly word-initial: prefixes that create an initial (even epenthetic) syllable are stressed, whereas a proclitic that creates an initial syllable is not, because it lies outside the phonological word (p. 127: 'Stress in Komnzo verbs is strictly word-initial and prefixes which create an initial syllable (even if filled with the epenthetic vowel) are stressed').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress only in words of more than three syllables; four-syllable words are ditrochees with secondary stress on syllable 3 (Table 2.9: nänzüthzsi [ˈnæⁿdʒʏθˌtsə̆si], kukufasi [ˈkukuˌɸasi], kdewawa [ˈkə̆ⁿdeˌwawa]). 'Words with more than four syllables vary in their assignment of secondary stress. Most five-syllable words assign secondary stress to the third syllable, but some assign it to the fourth. Most six-syllable and seven-syllable words assign secondary stress to the fourth syllable, but there are also exceptions. [..] The nature of secondary stress in Komnzo remains to be investigated in more detail.' (p. 72)
new_statements.exceptions: 'There are some exceptions to initial stress. For example, in partial reduplication (§4.2) the first syllable is unstressed, as in rrokar [rə̆ˈrokar] "things". In full reduplication, we find initial stress rokarrokar [ˈrokarˌrokar] [..]. Another example comes from verbs with a proclitic. In the verb form bŋatrakwr [bə̆ˈŋatrakʷə̆r] "s/he falls there", the proclitic b= (med) attaches to the outer layer of the fully inflected verb. Cases like partial reduplication and verbal proclitics should be seen as exceptions to the rule of initial stress.' (p. 71). Also p. 70: in monosyllabic CrV(C) roots realised with an epenthetic vowel, 'stress does not shift to the initial epenthetic vowel but remains with the specified vowel' (srak [ˈsɾak] ~ [sə̆ˈɾak]).
new_statements.identity_note: Döhler 2018 describes Komnzo, the Rouku-village variety of the Wára [tci] cluster (the catalog's 'Komnzo doculect'). Döhler treats Komnzo, Wára, Anta, Wèré and Kémä as closely related varieties of one language chain; his stress statement is explicitly about Komnzo. The unopened Wurm & Sarsa OPD would describe Wára proper (probably the Yokwa area); whether its stress placement is the same is unverified here.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Wára is predominantly penultimate: in polysyllabic words main stress 'usually' falls on the penult, with unspecified cases of final or antepenultimate stress; no lexical tone and no phonemic length; the epenthetic vowel that breaks initial CC clusters is not counted as a syllable nucleus and is unstressed ([kʌˈmɑm], [rɜˈmɑ]).
new_statements.exceptions: 'sometimes on the ultimate or antepenultimate syllable' (no conditioning given, no examples); epenthetic transition vowels in clusters are outside the stress count; vowels /e æ o/ diphthongise in stressed syllables of emphatic/careful speech (p. 9).
new_statements.identity_note: Döhler 2018 (catalog source) describes Komnzo, the variety of Rouku village. The OPD describes 'the Wára language (as defined by the present writer)', which 'comprises Wurm's Upper Peremka (Rouku) Language and, in part, Tonda Language', population c. 800, major villages Yékwa, Tékwa, Réku, Wámnefér, Ufaruwa (title page); Döhler treats Wára (Yokwa) and Komnzo (Rouku) as distinct but mutually intelligible varieties of the same dialect chain, all under glottocode wara1294 (Anta-Komnzo-Wára-Wérè-Kémä).

readall_conflicts: The one work hunted here (Wurm & Sarsa 2009 [2001], OPD Wára, listed twice in the bibliography) CONTRADICTS the catalog placement at the doculect level: the catalog record for wara1294 is the Komnzo doculect coded fixed initial (stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable)) from Döhler 2018 §2.4.5 ('Primary stress.. is assigned to the initial syllable of a word.. Stress is assigned from left to right. Words with two, three, and four syllables construct a trochee, dactyl, and ditrochee', pp. 6). The two agree on disyllables (10), on the absence of lexical tone and phonemic length, and on unstressed epenthetic vowels in initial clusters; they differ for words of three or more syllables (100 vs 010). Döhler's statement is the detailed one (acoustic correlates, templatic table, listed exceptions: partial reduplication, verbal proclitics) and concerns Komnzo (Rouku); Sarsa's is a one-sentence impressionistic statement for Wára (Yékwa/Yokwa and neighbouring villages, by his definition also covering Wurm's Upper Peremka (Rouku)). Recommended staging: keep the Komnzo record as is and add a doculect-level note/record 'Wára (Sarsa OPD 2001): penultimate, usually' for review rather than overwrite.
